clue.text: Land: survey somebody 'ad compiled all right

indicators.note: compiled suggests putting material together afresh, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

parts.note: OK is the everyday short form of all right

explanation.surface: Someone has thrown together a property survey and pronounced it fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compiled' rearranges SOMEBODYAD into DOMESDAYBO; the dropped aitch in 'ad is just there to supply the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Domesday record was William the Conqueror's 1086 survey of English landholding.

parts.note: computers work in numerical form, and fingers are the body's digits, so finger marks fed into a computer suit the word on both counts

explanation.surface: A question about police records stored on computer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means using numbers, as computers do, and also relating to fingers, the hand's digits.

clue.text: Sort of coat put on in afternoon?

definitions.meaning: a knitted jacket for a baby carries this name
a play staged in the afternoon is a daytime performance

explanation.surface: Someone slips on a particular coat after lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' reads as dressing, but in the second sense it means staging a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby's knitted jacket is called this kind of coat, and an afternoon theatre performance has the same name.

indicators.note: transposed means two parts swap places, so the first word is moved behind the second

parts.note: the old music-hall song Daisy Bell is about a bicycle built for two, so it is a song about a cycle

explanation.surface: Someone has rearranged a tune called Daisy into a musical piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy Bell ('Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer do') is a famous song about a bicycle; 'transposed' sounds musical but just swaps the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of songs meant to be performed together as one connected work forms a musical sequence.

clue.text: Long: range needed by American destroyers:

indicators.note: needed by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Ships need a long reach to do their job.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American mountain chain is the longest continental range in the world.

indicators.note: in a down clue, top puts the mountain word above the rest

parts.note: Ben is the Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis

indicators.note: changes tells us the letters of the following word are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Heat at a mountain summit shifts lower down the slopes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' places BEN first; 'changes' turns HEAT into EATH.
explanation.definitionFit: Something situated under another thing is lower down than it.

definitions.meaning: crossword sense of something that flows, a river
one of the furry litter-collecting creatures in the British children's books and TV series

explanation.surface: A flower belonging to the Wombles of Wimbledon Common.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a river (it flows): this one is in Venezuela. The Wombles are a British children's TV series about burrowing creatures who tidy up Wimbledon Common.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a great South American river and also the name of a plump, lazy Womble character.

clue.text: Crystal-clear results' of their inflationary: practices ?. .

definitions.text: Crystal-clear results' of their inflationary: practices

parts.words: Crystal-clear results' of their inflationary: practices
parts.note: inflationary sounds like economics, but these craftsmen inflate molten material with their breath to make clear vessels

explanation.surface: An economist's sneer that the effects of some policy are plain for all to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Craftsmen who shape molten material by puffing into a tube produce crystal vessels.

parts.note: light work is easy work
E is east, a compass direction
N is north, a second compass direction

explanation.surface: Simple instructions for slimming.
explanation.walkthrough: Two compass points, E and N, follow LIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something less heavy is to reduce its weight.

parts.note: Mozart's opera hero is Don Giovanni, and being like a don, an Oxbridge academic, means scholarly and bookish

explanation.surface: Someone is compared to the notorious seducer of Mozart's opera.
explanation.walkthrough: In British universities a don is a college lecturer, so the adjective means pedantically academic.
explanation.definitionFit: Being like a university lecturer means being scholarly and pedantic.

clue.text: He fell for gypsy drink. (not egg-flip though)

definitions.text: He fell for gypsy drink. (not egg-flip though)

parts.words: He fell for gypsy drink. (not egg-flip though)
parts.note: the nursery-rhyme egg who had a great fall shares his name with an old drink of ale boiled with brandy; the egg-flip aside teases his eggshell

explanation.surface: A man fell for a gypsy's drink, though not an eggy one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fell for' looks like 'was taken in by', but the nursery-rhyme character literally fell off a wall. An egg-flip is an eggnog-style drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The egg-shaped nursery-rhyme figure fell from a wall, and his name was also given to a strong old ale drink.

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from William Blake's poem known as Jerusalem, sung as a hymn in England

explanation.surface: A quotation from Blake's Jerusalem with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake's lines, now the hymn Jerusalem, ask whether Jerusalem was built here among these dark mills of the devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake called the industrial mills devilish, belonging to the Prince of Darkness.

parts.note: the main is the open ocean, and capacity is space, so this is space on the ocean for a ship to steer

explanation.surface: A phrase about the chief ability needed for military exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like 'chief' but is the poetic word for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors use the term for open water with enough space for a ship to turn safely.

indicators.note: say signals that the word spoken out loud sounds like the answer

parts.note: a church tower's bell is something that waits to be rung

explanation.surface: A lovely young woman waits for an engagement ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a woman hoping for a proposal; the wordplay is a thing struck to ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A beautiful woman, especially the loveliest at a party, is a beauty.

clue.text: Modified card game for the desperado

definitions.meaning: a version of bridge for three players, adapted from the usual four-handed game

explanation.surface: A rule-tweaked card game is the choice of an outlaw.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both a three-handed variant of bridge and a vicious killer ready for anything.

parts.note: to test is to try out
a match has a head that bursts into flame when struck

explanation.surface: A competition to test a would-be hothead.
explanation.walkthrough: A test match is an international cricket game; 'hothead' is a match head that can catch fire.
explanation.definitionFit: An international cricket or rugby fixture between national sides is a major contest.

clue.text: Veterans needing a wind to keep them going

definitions.text: needing a wind to keep them going
definitions.meaning: old-fashioned clocks have to be wound regularly to keep ticking

explanation.surface: Elderly people who need a breather to carry on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a wind' suggests breath for tired old folk, but it is winding up old clocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Long-serving people are veterans, and old clocks, which need winding, are timepieces of the past.

parts.note: In brief sounds like 'to sum up', but a lawyer's brief is a bundle of documents on a case

explanation.surface: A short summary of today's newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: A file of documents about a person or case is a bundle of papers.

definitions.meaning: read as two words, something pictured in one's fancy, existing only in the imagination

explanation.surface: Someone's early years were only make-believe.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as IN FANCY to get the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the earliest stage of life, and split in two it means existing in the imagination.

parts.note: the word can mean with the skeleton taken out, as in fish prepared for cooking, or stiffened with stays, as in a corset

explanation.surface: A fishmonger asks whether the fish is to be prepared.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means stripped of bones, yet a corset so described has bones put in, so it can mean both.

clue.text: Thraldom in the, time of James

indicators.note: the time of James puts the time word after the name

parts.note: James Bond is Ian Fleming's secret agent
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: Serfdom in the days of King James.
explanation.walkthrough: James suggests a Stuart king, but it is the spy Bond; 'of' places AGE after BOND.
explanation.definitionFit: Thraldom is slavery or servitude, being held in chains.

parts.note: pay-out suggests a cashier, but here it is paying people out, getting revenge, which a Greek goddess embodied

explanation.surface: A legendary woman who hands out wages.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of retribution punished pride, paying wrongdoers back.

indicators.note: says the letters of the following words could be rearranged into the answer

explanation.surface: Asking what would put America at ease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What might make' rearranges the letters of USA FEEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word for restful and soothing, giving comfort.

clue.text: Of course, better actor misses lead part

indicators.note: misses says the actor word goes without a letter

parts.note: a player is an actor on stage

indicators.note: lead points at the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Naturally, a stronger actor loses the starring role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misses' drops P, the lead of 'part', from PLAYER. 'Of course, better' is a bookmaker at a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookmaker who takes bets at a racecourse is a betting professional there.

clue.text: Note mother: sharing a thousand — one can't have less

parts.note: a minim is a musical note, a half note

indicators.note: sharing says the two pieces have one letter in common and overlap on it

parts.note: mum is a familiar name for mother
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: A note says mother is splitting a thousand pounds and nobody can get less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sharing a thousand' means MINIM and MUM share one M, so the second M is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: The least possible amount is the point below which nobody can go.

clue.text: River goes round another small wood'

indicators.note: goes round says the first river encloses the second

parts.note: the Spey is a river in Scotland, famed for salmon and whisky
the Inn is another river, flowing through Innsbruck in Austria

explanation.surface: A river bends round another small wood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' means another river, the Inn; 'goes round' puts INN inside SPEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A small thicket or copse of trees is a little wood.

clue.text: How 'to get across that art isn't peculiar:

indicators.note: peculiar means odd, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Explaining how that art is not odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiar' rearranges ART ISNT; 'that' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Passage from one side to the other, the means of crossing, is this.

clue.text: They keep turning up in Tibet

definitions.text: They keep turning up in Tibet

parts.words: They keep turning up in Tibet
parts.note: turning up sounds like appearing often, but Buddhist devotional cylinders are literally spun round

explanation.surface: Something keeps appearing all over Tibet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tibetan Buddhists spin cylinders holding written prayers, each turn counting as a recitation.
